Let's produce a clear answer.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>**Photosynthesis – the two main stages** | Stage | Where it happens | Primary inputs | Primary outputs | |-------|------------------|---------------|-----------------| | **1. Light‑dependent reactions (photophosphorylation)** | **Thylakoid membranes** inside the chloroplast; the light‑absorbing pigments (photosystems I & II) are embedded in these membranes. | • Light (visible spectrum, ~600 nm)
• Water (H₂O) or, in some organisms, Ca²⁺, Na⁺, etc.
• NADP⁺ (the redox carrier)
• ADP + inorganic phosphate (Pi) for ATP synthesis | • Molecular oxygen (O₂) released into the atmosphere (by splitting water)
• Reduced NADPH (NADPH + 2 H⁺)
• ATP (from ATP synthase) made by oxidative phosphorylation of the electron transport chain | | **2. Light‑independent reactions (Calvin–Benson cycle)** | **Stroma** (the fluid-filled space around the thylakoids). The enzymes that condense CO₂ to sugars are located in the stroma. | • Carbon **dioxide (CO₂)** from the air
• ATP (the chemiosmotic “energy currency”) generated in the light reactions
• NADPH (the reducing power) generated in the light reactions | • 3‑phosphoglycerate (3‑PGA) that is oxidized/reduced and then transformed into glyceraldehyde‑3‑phosphate, eventually forming glucose, starch, or other carbohydrates. (The cycle does not directly release O₂; instead it uses the O₂ that was produced earlier.) | ### Quick mental diagram ``` Thylakoid membranes: Light photons → Photo‑electrons → PSI – PSII --> ATP (via chemiosmosis) + NADPH + O₂ Stroma (outside the phospholipid bilayer): O₂ produced in thylakoids travels freely; Calvin cycle self‑conditions CO₂ + ATP + NADPH → H₂O (return to water) + sugars ``` --- **Key take‑aways** - **Light‑dependent stage** (in the thylakoid membrane) converts solar energy into **ATP** and **NADPH**, while **splitting water** returns electrons and releases **oxygen**. - **Calvin cycle** (in the stroma) consumes **CO₂**, **ATP** and **NADPH** to build **permanent carbon compounds** (e.g., sugars, starch), providing the energy sources that support all other life on Earth.
